item.title: Everything You Need To Know About Ink Drops in Disney Lorcana
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|competitive

Everything You Need To Know About Ink Drops in Disney Lorcana

Deckbuilding will never be the same

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 8, 2026

|

14 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's a very rare thing for a new mechanic to threaten our entire understanding of a trading card game. Once a game moves past the first few booster sets, you tend to find the foundational aspects are baked in and hard to usurp. Disney Lorcana has decided that it doesn't want to play the game that way — anything but. 

Ink drops are about to change the rules of Disney Lorcana and you need to be ready for them. 

If you haven't been following the reveal season leading into Hyperia City, you may not be familiar with what an ink drop is. Ink drops are a new token type that can be created by a menagerie of cards, each of which provides you with a temporary ink. Once you use one it's removed from the game forever. 

This is an absurdly flexible resource. You can stockpile these tokens until it's time to cash in on something huge, accelerate towards a card ahead of time or simply let them fill in for a card you don't want to ink. We saw the power of Sail the Azurite Sea jumping straight to four ink for well over a year and that's the floor on a card like Another Tale to Spin. 

The thing is? That's not all you can do. Hyperia City contains cards that reward you for spending ink drops on them, allowing your new resource to be converted into card draw, additional stats or bonus effects. You'll need to balance these upsides against the power of acceleration and that makes for a wonderful new deckbuilding puzzle. 

I cannot understate how impactful this new mechanic is going to be. Deckbuilding fundamentally changes solely off the existence of ink drops, because you can consistently play on odd numbers/even numbers of ink if you consistently generate ink drops. Mapping out how each color can create ink drops will inform which other cards are playable going forward. This is very emblematic of previous Sapphire deckbuilding to me, but I'm excited to see what it's no longer limited to one color. 

At my count, there are 45 cards in Hyperia City that care about (or create) an ink drop. I want to pinpoint a few of the most impressive ones in each ink and work through what they enable after the release of Hyperia City. 

Amber

We're starting with Amber because it has the least options for ink drops by far. Personally, I think this is deliberate. You can accent Amber with a different ink if you want acceleration, or you can lean into existing tools like Grandmother Willow - Ancient Advisor or Lantern if jumping from two to four is your goal. 

Port Authority - Center Hub is an interesting one. It reads a little awkward to provide the bonus to both players for the work that you're doing, but I haven't forgotten how potent McDuck Manor - Scrooge's Mansion and The Queen's Castle - Mirror Chamber used to be. The stat line on this is very powerful despite it being uninkable.

I'm concerned because it doesn't bridge naturally into Raging Storm, which is the biggest Amber tool I want to accelerate into. If you play Port Authority on turn four, you can move a character into it on turn five to jump to six ink. This only puts you to seven ink on turn six and forces you to have a character in play that'll get swept up by Raging Storm when you play it.

You could play it on turn five and immediately move in a character to fix this? Perhaps you should accelerate into Stitch - Carefree Surfer instead? Unsure. 

In contrast, I think Mickey Mouse - Best in Town is a bit of a beast. It's possible that it fixes the curve issues with Port Authority while providing you with a cheap character to move into it. It may be a hot take, but I think Mickey is much better in a control shell than an aggressive one despite the two lore pips. 

If your opponent is wasting time clearing Mickey, it is buying you the time you want to reach your inevitability. If you're an aggressive deck, you also probably cannot use the ink drops you're generating as well as your opponent. I think there's a lot of power in putting your opponent between a rock and a hard place like this. You either keep questing away... or wreck the opposing counterplay with an opposing Raging Storm. 

Both of these cards have me interested in playing on odds. A Mickey Mouse - Best in Town on turn one allows you to jump to any odd number you like if it's staying alive, while Port Authority is essentially just moving your ink forward a turn. That has me looking at cards like Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty and Cheshire Cat - Inexplicable as other cards that may make for good haymakers. 

Amethyst 

Amethyst gets significantly more ink drop synergies — eight cards, in fact. However, I expect most of the deckbuilding here to revolve around Madam Mim - Resourceful Trickster.

Mim is the payoff. Immediately drawing two cards on play is quite powerful but drawing additional cards every turn you remove an ink drop leads to an obscene snowball. I believe this is an effect worth building around, so I'm looking for other cards that both accelerate to eight cleanly and generate repeatable ink drops. 

Merlin - Profoundly Curious is far-and-away the obvious stalwart here. In a vacuum, the card is powerful enough on its own, threatening to draw cards as it quests and bridge you directly to six. It also enables the Christmasland scenario of shifting into Merlin - Ink Drop Tinkerer to take you to a theoretical nine ink on turn six. 

That means you're jamming Madam Mim and scoring value from both abilities in the same turn with any one cost card. I'm just expecting this card to see a lot of play either way. 

Inkcaster Skates is very interesting to me. It's one of the few repeatable ways to generate ink drops in the game. Assuming you activate it on turn three when playing it, it'll also allow you to reach eight ink on turn five. That's absolutely perfect for Madam Mim! It's not big or flashy, but I think it has some potential. 

I've also seen a few people talking about Higitus Figitus, but I can't say I'm a believer in this one. Six ink is just so much solely jump your ink drop count. I find myself wishing this card had Sing Together, but frankly that may have been a little bit too good. 

Emerald

Emerald also seems to be quite interested in ink drops, with a hefty nine cards that care about the new mechanic. Interestingly, two of these cards were given epic rarity counterparts, each of which direct you into one of the different directions you can take with Emerald. 

You can jump from two to four like a Bollywood version of Sail the Azurite Sea and Tipo - Growing Son, or you can lean into item synergies and jump up to seven. 

Another Tale to Spin and Molly Cunningham - Remembers to Share are the no-questions-asked accelerants on turn two assuming you don't mind offering an ink drop to your opponent. While this will come back to bite you on occasion, I do think you can build your deck in a way to better abuse the acceleration with a high density of four cost characters. 

Shere Khan - Opportunistic Tycoon and Merlin - Profoundly Curious seem like a wonderful fit to continue up the curve, but maybe something like Cinderella - Ballroom Sensation also tickles your fancy. It seems very easy to daisy-chain from two-to-four-to-six. 

Go Go Tomago - Extreme Tester can achieve the similar thing without providing ink to the opponent but requires them to pick her off in a challenge in order to secure your ink. I think this makes her a better fit in an aggressively slanted deck that can punish with a five-cost card if the opponent tries to slow her down more so than a guaranteed accelerant. This is Business and Kit Cloudkicker - Irrepressible Bear might fit into a shell like that nicely as well. 

The other angle of attack seems to be item focused. Baymax - Lab Assistant is a demon if you can consistently activate it, jumping you straight to a seven-ink turn on turn five. That's a magic number for threats like Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty or Hades - Infernal Schemer. Even if there isn't quite enough in the chamber just yet, I feel like this card is priced to move. 

Honey Lemon - Testing the Limits isn't the set championship promo card by accident. This is a turbo-fixed spin on Hiram Flaversham - Toymaker, one of the only cards to be banned in the history of Lorcana. The math gets a little weird here because you can play items either before or after Honey Lemon to fuel her ability, changing which numbers you'll want to focus on hitting. Cheap items will make you play smoother on odd numbers, which can be a huge boon for a different item payoff like Ariel - Collector of Oddities... but that's less true if you banished a Blinding Chem Ball. Suddenly, you begin to see all the permutations here. 

I think Bobby Zimuruski - Soundboard Whiz is mostly its own little sidequest. Assuming you have one Bobby and one Leaning Tower of Cheese-a, this can be a quite way to jump up on odd numbers too. Maybe that makes it good enough to enable Baymax, too. 

Ruby 

There's something horrific about the implications of Tadashi Hamada - Making Waves needing to be banished to make ink drops. Does he die again in this card? Can we stop wishing ill on poor Tadashi?! 

Ruby falls on the lower side of ink drop compatibility right now with only five tools to choose from. That being said, I think it may have some of the stronger glue pieces in Meilin Lee - Ecstatic Fan, Pushing Boundaries, and Wasabi - Called into Battle. 

Pushing Boundaries isn't that exciting: it's just yet another way to always jump from two to four ink, which is noteworthy alongside those Emerald cards that were looking to do the same. It just happens to scale a little better into the late game to give you some insulation in an otherwise-problematic challenge. 

Tadashi Hamada is a little more interesting. There's not a ton of ways to secure two ink drops in one burst because it's such a huge jump in resources. This one can't really be ignored because it's questing for three and happily crashes into an opposing character to turbocharge your way up to Madam Mim - Resourceful Trickster or Raging Storm. It's not gigantic, but it's worth thinking about. 

In contrast, I really like Wasabi - Called into Battle. If you're jumping up on even numbers, this is a great play to extend your board and not use up your ink drop, keeping that bottom effect active. If you can do that, this almost plays like a fixed Mulan - Elite Archer: a card that was almost good enough several times between Ursula's Return and Azurite Sea. I'm quite excited to explore what this card can do. 

Sapphire

It shouldn't be a huge surprise that the infamous ink acceleration color gets a decent slice of the ink drop pie. There are eight cards worth watching in Sapphire for all your ink drop shenanigans, helmed by the signpost that is Baymax - Amped Up. 

 

Obviously, the intended play pattern here is to generate two ink drops with Baymax - Lab Assistant, then immediately shift into the gigantic 5/8 character that converts future ink drops into permanent ink. Personally, I think this is very good. It might be "worth building around" levels of good, especially since Emerald Sapphire would give you access to Honey Lemon - Testing the Limits alongside Blinding Chem Ball, Prototype Chem Ball and Honey Lemon - Ingenious Researcher to buy them back. This is clearly an intended archetype. 

There are a few other standouts here though. A Dark Age No More is what I expected Sapphire to get: the ol' double acceleration. This card really has me looking at solid six-cost cards that I can punish the opponent with way ahead of schedule. Demona - Scourge of the Wyvern Clan immediately comes to mind, but even the aforementioned Wasabi - Called into Battle might be a good place to go. 

I'm going to try and brute force Powerline - World's Greatest Rock Star again and figure out the rest later. There's a lot to like here and I expect the card to do some work. 

In contrast to his Ruby counterpart, I think I'm going to find myself hating Wasabi - Future Thinker. We have seen boardwide Ward be disturbingly potent in the past, and Ward as a whole is clearly quite good at the moment — that's why Emerald Sapphire Mouse House is performing so admirably. Adding that effect with a dose of resist thanks to a 5/5 two-lore character feels like it has potential. I just won't be the one exploring it! 

Finally, we have to note Intense Research. If you're spending an ink drop on this card, it's just Visions of the Future. That card was a tried-and-true staple during almost its entire tenure in Core Constructed and I expect the same from Intense Research if ink drops are plentiful. You just have to build your deck as to not use your ink drops on other cards. 

Steel

I saved the big one until last. There are an astounding thirteen cards in Steel that interact with ink drops and some of them are absolute haymakers. We'd be remiss if we didn't begin the discussions with the tiger in the room: Shere Khan - Khan Industries CEO. 

This card is a monster. I have it pegged as one of the best in the set. "New Incentive" enables some backbreaking blowouts alongside characters like Cheshire Cat - Inexplicable, and "Corner the Market" will almost always score you an ink drop on the turn Shere Khan is played because of it. 

That means its removal, acceleration and stats all baked into a single card... which is ridiculous. Curving Shere Khan into Demona - Scourge of the Wyvern Clan is going to be disgusting, but you're going to have to get used to it. 

Khan Transport Delivery is yet another means of "sailing" up to four ink on turn three, but it might be the one that's closest to Sail the Azurite Sea on account of replacing itself. I also think Ink Explosion might be a bit of an underappreciated gem in a world with so many ways to jump to four ink. Consider the following: 

  • Turn 1: Mickey Mouse - Best in Town 
  • Turn 2: Khan Transport Delivery. Quest with Mickey
  • Turn 3: Ink Explosion the first answer to Mickey. Quest with Mickey
  • Turn 4: Prince Charming - Protector of the Realm (or frankly any seven-cost character!) 

It's not always going to come up this way, but I do expect Ink Explosion to remove a threat and refund the ink drop you spend on turn three reasonably often, opening up deckbuilding space for five-cost options like Broadway - Sturdy and Strong too. I'm a big fan of the possibilities here! 

I also think that Marie - Caught in the Act might be the most dangerous ink drop generator of them all. The little kitten not only enables ink from turn two onwards with effects like The Terror that Flaps in the Night, but the card will also be online every time a wayward Strength of a Raging Fire stamps out an opposing character. I think sequencing with Marie is going to be very important, but the card is clearly very strong. 

Closing Thoughts

...and breathe! 

That's a healthy chunk of information to process about ink drops and their various cards. Hopefully the eternal whirring of my mind will help your early deckbuilding attempts with ink drops in mind. 

Be sure to let me know how you get on! If you've got further questions, let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: Revealing The Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel Event Deck
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|Ultimate Pit Fight|news

Revealing The Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel Event Deck

Multiplayer chaos returns to Flesh and Blood on October 30th 2026 — and TCGplayer is excited to bring you exclusive reveals from the product!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 20, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's entirely possible that your introduction to Flesh and Blood didn't include Ultimate Pit Fight. If you ask me, that's a crying shame. 

Flesh and Blood's social play format has been a little underserved by an ecosystem so influenced by competitive play. The game prides itself on one of the most robust organized play circuits in the TCG industry and a steady foundation for local play, but it hasn't much tapped into my visceral need to smash the heads of my friends around a kitchen table and engage in utter nonsense. 

That changes today. 

The inaugural Smash Palace was a great start, but Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel is an entirely different beast. This multiplayer box set pits various Warrior heroes against each other to determine the true master of the blade, all backed by the resounding success that is Mastery Pack: Warrior. 

Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel is the perfect introductory product for a small group of friends looking to get into Flesh and Blood, or an enfranchised crew with some grudges to settle. Thanks to Crack, Shuffle, Play! design, each player can simply open three packs, shuffle them together, choose a hero and get straight into the action! You can treat it like a boardgame and play with the same decks or pick up additional packs of Mastery Pack: Warrior to play all over again.

But outside of the warrior theme, what makes Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel stand out from its predecessor? I'm glad you ask, corporeal voice on the internet: It's the heroes and the event deck — the latter of which I'm revealing to you in this article! 

I wanted to take a moment to highlight both Zane, Broadly Beloved and Killjoy, the Crooked Blade before I do so, though. Both heroes are brand new to Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel and perfectly capture the Revered and Reviled gameplay that emerged in Super Slam: the perfect hero-villain dynamic for a multiplayer format. Even better, both heroes are legal in Silver Age, so you'll have the ability to dive deeper into them in constructed formats. 

I'm a bit of a sucker for the Thief class, so I'm gonna have to try cracking Killjoy. I'm reliably informed that there's plenty of Zane fans in the audience too. 

But enough stalling! You want to see the types of chaos can unfold during a game with Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel! The team at Legend Story Studios have already revealed the wonderful Unleash Pandemonium, Eeny, Meeny, Trained Saurian, Pint with a Pal and Visit the Crystal Ball, but it's my pleasure to bring you the rest of the event deck. 

I'll be adding those previously revealed cards into this article as images just so that every card in the deck is pictured below. I also kinda wanna yap about them. Check it out! 

First, we've got the "Tourney" equipment set, which will jump out and equip themselves to you if you're lucky enough to find one. If you've already got the equipment slot in question filled, you'll get to respin from the event deck again to avoid missing out on something flashy. 

Each of these has a unique effect attached that can swing a game in your favor. That could be an explosive barrage of additional event cards, or some cheeky bonus damage on your weapon attacks as an attack reaction. Either way, it's all upside. 

Sale at the Golden Anvil concludes the majestic lineup of event deck cards with a way to repurchase your equipment. It's worth noting that the "Tourney" set doesn't go to your graveyard, so it isn't eligible for this effect. You also need to remember that this sale isn't exclusive to you! You may score the Gold when the event flips up, but you don't get exclusive access to all these sick deals. 

The other three cards in this gallery had already been revealed, so they shouldn't be too much of a surprise to you. That said, Unleash Pandemonium is exactly what I want from a bomb going off. Each turn that goes by that it remains in the event deck leads you closer and closer to the most absurd turn cycle you've ever seen. 

Gold can become a quickly contested resource in Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel, especially once Killjoy starts getting her mitts into your money. Cutpurse Generosity helps to both refill your cash… but also lets the thief at the table pilfer a token from you. Den of Thieves causes a similar level of debauchery, but it also double dips into the event deck for another dose. 

Eeny Meenie has already been revealed, but it's a particularly nasty event that'll force you to make an enemy. I already love the tension in choosing which of your neighbors to attack, but you'll have some explaining to do if you don't at least attempt to secure both additional rewards. But if you do? Well, you risk upsetting two opponents instead! 

If you're desperate for some extra currency, Ezy Sqeez Bookie Syndicate has you covered! Simply make a wager with an opponent and score some damage to be rewarded for your bet. With some careful social politics, they might even take a dive for you. Perhaps you can deliberately lose to get some Gold into their hands? Who could possibly say? 

You may notice a theme at this stage: Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel is packed with so many more events that reveal additional cards from the event deck, causing each flip at the beginning of the turn to have a much higher ceiling. Hit the Top and On the Front Foot continue this pattern, while Flip the Balance of Battle provides an absurd burst of additional damage that an opponent(s) must defend to prevent it snowballing.

Ire of the Crowd is the other side of that coin. You don't want to see this one, because your opponents will be incentivized to keep you out at all costs. What? You thought you had control of the game? Unlucky, you smarmy idiot. 

If you've fallen victim to the Ire of the Crowd, Regain Momentum is the type of event that can re-open the door for you, providing a sharpened weapon and another event to get you back in the fight. Reverse Psychology fills a similar niche, draining life away to help level the playing field. Pint with a Pal can also help drag your life total back into the realm of safe, especially if you can target a Reviled hero who won't benefit from the cheering quite as much as you! 

Start Swinging may be my favorite event in the deck. This thing is going to get the fireworks going. Everybody has Go Again. Everybody can attack with their weapon multiple times. Buckle up buttercup, the show is about to begin. 

Visit Smelter's Point and Visit Blade's Edge both offer you additional ways to sharpen your weapon with a little bit of gravy on top. Personally, I think the cost reduction from Visit Blade's Edge is often more dangerous, but Visit Smelter's Point could always reveal Visit Blade's Edge as well. How sharp would you like your weapon to be before sinking it into my skull, eh? 

If you choose to Visit the Winner Takes All instead, you'd better be ready to gamble. This event applies to ALL attacks, so Flurry tokens or Go Again can lead to some dangerous wagers fast. If the opponent refuses to defend you or gets caught by an untimely attack reaction, they'll find the entire content of their bank account swiftly in your hands. It's an aptly named event and an incredibly swingy one at that. 

Last but not least (that's just how the alphabet works!) we've got Windmill Spin. This snazzy little event can be backbreaking if you chose to take a bunch of damage to really swing for the hills this turn, but can be a real liability if you intended to play a small hand after some timely defense. That wager isn't optional, so you'll be risking the gift of Gold with every enemy at the table. 

Closing Thoughts

Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel seems stuffed with ways to get your brain spinning. There are so many events that reward you for keeping your cards… but so many other events that really incentivize you to deny damage from your opponent by giving up those cards. Each game should play differently regardless of card pool and provide a social, political play environment for any Flesh and Blood players chasing that experience. 

Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel releases at your local game store on October 30th 2026. If you'd like to secure a box for your friends, pre-orders are also available now on the TCGplayer marketplace with many GEM stores. If you've already purchased a surplus of Mastery Pack: Warrior, you can also purchase the event deck by itself and get to some Crack, Shuffle and Play! 

Thank you to Legend Story Studios for the opportunity to reveal this event deck. If you have any further questions, feel free to hit me up at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky.  Alternatively, feel free to check out my other work here on TCGplayer for another slice of everything nice about your favorite trading card game. 

But until next time, I've been HowlingMines. You've been amazing. 

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: Hide & Sneak Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)
item.description:
Pokémon|competitive

Hide & Sneak Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)

A hidden gem that's sneakily good.

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Oct 20, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Pokémon Deck Guides

Hide & Sneak is one of the newer decks in the format, and while it hadn't seen much success at tournaments, Rahul Reddy took this deck to a Top 4 placement at the Louisville Regional Championships, showing that it can compete at a top level! This archetype feels tailor-made to counter Dragapult ex decks, and while Dragapult players do have a lot of counterplay, the single-Prize nature give it a lot of game into the other matchups!

Hide & Sneak Deck Guide

The Hide & Sneak deck is built off the Hide & Sneak Pokémon, and the synergy they have with Dhelmise. The Hide & Sneak ability is only on Shuppet, Banette, Poltchageist and Sinistcha and they usually just get sent to the discard pile, but being unaffected by effects of opposing attacks and abilities can be really impactful. It protects these Pokémon from the residual damage from Dragapult's Phantom Dive, Munkidori's Adrena-Brain and Alakazam's Powerful Hand. Once you discard four Pokémon with the Hide & Sneak ability, Dhelmise's Vengeful Anchor attack gets buffed from 30 damage to 170 damage for just one Psychic Energy. This hits for enough to two-hit KO almost any Pokémon in the format, and with a Lillie's Clefairy ex in play, you can take a one-hit KO on Dragapult ex thanks to the Fairy Zone ability. All the Psychic Pokémon are searchable with Telepathic Psychic Energy, and you can even search Shuppet to set up a potential Puppet Pull to establish your hand.

The main goal of this deck is so discard the four Hide & Sneak Pokémon then chain Dhelmise for the rest of the game. You use Legacy Energy as the ACE SPEC to manipulate the Prize trade and remove the downside of using multiple two-Prize Pokémon, but I think there's a ton of merit to including other ACE SPECs such as Secret Box or Prime Catcher. One of the main advantages of playing the Hide & Sneak deck is that you get to use a ton of draw engines, and you have an additional draw supporter alongside Lillie's Determination with Gywnn, which has the additional use of discarding your Hide & Sneak Pokémon as well as drawing extra cards. This deck also has Prism Tower as the Stadium; while it only draws one card, it does allow you to discard extra Hide and Sneak Pokémon. This deck also includes Explorer's Guidance as another early game supporter to help you discard cards.

To help with draw cards, this deck it also includes a small Dudunsparce line. Run Away Draw can be looped multiple times throughout the game to see more and more cards, but its real strength is being left in play to protect you from disruption like Special Red Card or Unfair Stamp. Dudunsparce ex is also an answer to the Basic Box matchup, which is relatively difficult because 170 is not enough to take one-hit knockouts, and they can remove your attacks with Chien-Pao's Snow Sink ability, discarding their Area Zero Underdepths and the damaged Basic Pokémon. Tenacious Tail will usually take a one-hit KO on a Pokémon ex, and both of the commonly played answers to Dudunsparce ex (Raging Bolt ex and Koraidon ex ASC) are weak to Psychic (or can be made so with Fairy Zone), which gives you a significant advantage in the Prize trade.

There's another direction you can take the Hide & Sneak deck that doesn't just involve attacking with Dhelmise. Sinistcha's Matcha Spin attack puts six damage counters on all your opponent's Pokémon as long as you have six Hide & Sneak Pokémon in your discard pile, and Spiritomb's Spiritual End quadruples the number of damage counters on two of your opponent's Pokémon if you have 13 Hide & Sneak Pokémon in your discard pile. You can only play a maximum of 16 Hide & Sneak Pokémon in your deck, which often prevents you from using the Dundunsparce line if you're intending to use Spiritual End. Both versions of this deck are solid, but there's not currently a consensus on which one is stronger.

Even without Spiritomb in your deck, you can still go for Matcha Spin, usually to clean up after a Vengeful Anchor. Since Matcha Spin hits Tera Pokémon while they're on the bench, you can often use it to set up multiple Basic Pokémon ex for a future Vengeful Anchor KO, or to wipe opposing boards of low HP Pokémon. A tech card that's sometimes seen in Hide & Sneak decks is Patrat, which prevents opposing Munkidoris from using their Adrena-Brain abilities, removing the option to heal while spreading damage with Matcha Spin. This doesn't come up a lot in the Dragapult matchup since you're usually intending to attack with Dhelmise, but there are situations where they can use the damage given to them by Risky Ruins to two-hit KO a Dhemise from the residual Phantom Dive damage. I'd consider saving the Legacy Energy for the Lillie's Clefairy in the Dragapult matchup, and you can also tech Lillie's Pearl for this matchup to further protect your Lillie's Clefairy, as the two main ways you can lose the Dragapult matchup are either through them chasing your Clefairy multiple times or them attacking with Fezandipiti ex and winning the Prize trade through it. If they're unable to attack with Fezandipiti early, I'd look for positions where you can take relevant Prize cards without benching Lillie's Clefairy, or try to bench it on turns where you know they can't play Boss's Orders and Phantom Dive in the same turn.

Hide & Sneak is one of the many single-Prize decks in the current format, and it's definitely on the rise! If you aren't playing this deck, be prepared for both versions of it and make sure you have a solid game plan into them!

item.title: 10 Underrated Yu-Gi-Oh Cards From Beyond the Brave You Need to Try
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|competitive

10 Underrated Yu-Gi-Oh Cards From Beyond the Brave You Need to Try

Look past The Great Gallant Bandit to find some really neat tech.

By Hanko Chow

|

Published Oct 21, 2026

|

9 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's hard to top the last core booster set with Chaos Origins introducing Extended Art variants in a main set as well as the meta-defining Light and Darkness Ritual archetype. With that being said, Beyond the Brave has a tough crowd to please, especially since it features Joey and his Dark Time Wizard strategy. There's definitely a gap between the power level of these sets but The Great Gallant Bandit is here to hold down the fort!

10 Underrated Cards You Missed From Beyond the Brave

Everyone wants a piece of The Great Gallant Bandit, but don't let one card take all of your attention away from the other interesting archetypes - most of them are viable in Genesys! Today, I'll quickly go over what bulk cards you should look into and keep an eye on in case they have more potential in the near future!

#10 Cartoon Shade

This little Illusion has some interesting features. From being a new Illusion type monster that can be searched by Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws or Nightmare Apprentice to being a "Toon" monster, it's just a matter of time before some decks will feature Cartoon Shade as some sort of bridge to search for another card.

As of right now, there aren't that many fantastic Ritual monsters that Cartoon Shade can search for aside from maybe Herald of Ultimateness, Futsu no Mitama no Mitsurugi or Cyberse Code Magician, but it might find a home in Drytron since all of their monsters are 2000 ATK monsters that cannot be Normal Summoned/Set.

#9 Spell Shattering Sword

Another Spell is added to the Light and Darkness Ritual lineup. Spell Shattering Sword is pretty strong as disruption since it can either destroy all Face-Up Spells your opponent controls, acting not only as a niche board wipe but also possibly preventing a Continuous, Field Spell or Pendulum from resolving an effect, or it can be a monster negate while dropping their ATK to zero.

Combined with the power of Chaos Magical Hats, you have a pretty strong lineup. By setting Spell Shattering Sword, Chaos Mystic Box and perhaps Waking the Dragon with the effect of the Hats, you're highly likely forcing your opponent to destroy one of them to trigger their awesome effect. While Spell Shattering Sword doesn't summon a monster, it'll go after another random card in your opponent's hand instead.

#8 Clown Crew Cappello

The latest Clown Crew member has joined the gauntlet, and with it, another method for the deck to summon out bodies or search certain cards. Most importantly, Clown Crew Cappello is a Pendulum that, when tributed, allows you to shuffle all Pendulums from the field and the Face-Up Extra Deck back to the Main Deck (or face-down Extra Deck for specific monsters). For some reason, Cappello doesn't shuffle back Pendulums from the graveyard like the other Clown Crew members do for their respective card type. Perhaps the designers never considered that Pendulums can go to the graveyard pretty often.

The main purpose of Clown Crew Cappello is its Pendulum Scale effect, which can send any non-Pendulum Clown Crew card from your deck to the graveyard. All of the Clown Crew Traps are the most useful ones to send, with Clown Crew Finale's tributing something to search another, Clown Crew New Face placing itself and Clown Crew Soiree Operations giving Clown Crew another Tribute Summon during any Main Phase. If you already have access to Clown Crew Malabarisme and Clown Crew Biancaviso, I think sending Clown Crew Soiree Operations could be very ideal to help give you more potential Tribute Summons!

After you tribute Cappello, whether it be from the field or hand, you can trigger its effect to summon one other Clown Crew member from your Deck or Extra Deck, giving you more ways to put out bodies. Another important note is that Clown Crew Cappello is a Level 4 monster which gives the deck another monster to Tribute Summon for in case you need to. While Cappello doesn't offer much on the field aside from lowering your opponent's defenses, there may be hope that they'll design another Clown Crew member to the family in the future. Another Tribute Summon would be great since only having Clown Crew Biancaviso as the Main boss monster feels pretty lackluster.

#7 and 6 Ashtra's Domain and Akasuna the Battle Ashtra

The newest archetype being introduced in Beyond the Brave is Ashtra, aSynchro-centric archetype revolving around Traps that can summon themselves as Tuners combined with these high-Level monsters that can summon themselves, reminiscent of Kashtiras.

Out of all the Ashtra cards, the first one that stands out is Ashtra's Domain since it's like a budget Solemn Accusation or Dark Bribe without giving your opponent a draw. It's a very simple generic Spell/Trap negate that can prove to be useful for any strategy. Just look at how the Dracotail Traps are used in other decks. Maybe this is just something you'll see in the Genesys format but I think for a local setting, you can probably get away with using Ashtra's Domain if you can't get Solemn Accusations. That is, until your opponents realize they can play around it by simply setting a card first before they play their Spell/Trap.

Akasuna the Battle Ashtra seems like a pretty strong card. With 3000 ATK points, an easy summoning condition and the ability to flip all your opponent's monsters face-down at the cost of another Trap card, there's so much potential for Ashtra. I just hope their next wave of support gives them a bright future.

#5, 4 and 3 New Destiny HERO or Dark Warrior cards!

HEROs is a fan favorite strategy, but that gets even better when it's Aster Phoenix's Destiny HEROs! Unlike the Elemental HEROs, Destiny HEROs focus around Dark Warriors with graveyard effects and unique boss monsters like the infamous Destiny HERO - Plasma. This time though, another boss monster gets retrained with Destiny HERO - Destro-Dogma, showcasing the classic Destiny HERO - Dogma holding the Cyclone Blade like it did in the anime!

This retrained version of Dogma is pretty cool actually since it's almost generic depending on the graveyard deck you're building. Since you can banish any three Warrior or Dark monsters to summon it from the hand or graveyard, Destro-Dogma makes sense to try in some milling Dark strategies. The 2000 effect damage plays well with the original Dogma effect but it's most important effect could be letting you Fusion Summon using monsters from your hand, field or graveyard! I can see this being a pretty neat option in Tearlaments or Lightsworns. I'll have to try and include it in a future deck.

One of the newest Fusions you can summon with Destro-Dogma could be Skyborne Blue Cularsaw! On summon, it equips either any monster from your opponent's graveyard or banishment, or a Warrior monster from your own graveyard/banishment, giving it the ability to negate a Spell/Trap by sending an Equip Card. It's a pretty neat option for Destiny HEROs but also a strong Super Polymerization option to be used against Destiny HEROs.

Speaking of Destiny HEROs and Fusion monsters, Destiny HERO - Dreadmaster has now evolved into Destiny HERO - Dreadnought Master. It can search search for any two cards that are Destiny HEROs or mention a specific Destiny HERO by name, which is pretty strong! This even gives you access to D - Force to make Destiny HERO - Plasma even better.

While you're most likely going to use Fusion Destiny to summon Destiny HERO - Destroyer Phoenix Enforcer most of the time, I wouldn't be surprised to see Destiny HERO - Dreadnought Master being summoned either since that double search can be so strong. But just like Skyborne Blue Cularsaw, this might just be another Super Polymerization target that other players will use against Destiny HERO players to beat Plasma and Destiny HERO - Destroyer Phoenix Enforcer, so make sure there's a Destiny HERO - Dark Angel on the opponent's field to prevent that from happening.

#2 CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon

Umbral Horror or Number 104: Masquerade has received a ton of Barian-related support cards in Beyond the Brave, but the one that stands out to me the most has to be the new Barian boss monster, CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon. Since the K9 cards make it very easy to summon N.As.H. Knight and CXyz N.As.Ch. Knight, that means you have easy access to those Number C101-107 monsters thanks to CXyz N.As.Ch. Knight. By summoning Number C101: Silent Honor DARK through the CXyz N.As.Ch. Knight's effect, you can then Xyz summon the new CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon on top!

You'll probably have a ton of Xyz Materials by the time you get to summon CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon which will give it a ton of ATK points. But most importantly, the continuous effect will be live to prevent the opponent from using their search effects. Similar to Thunder Dragon Colossus or DoomZ Destruction, this one-sided Mistake may just be K9's newest end board piece to floodgate the opponent out of their deck.

#1 Elemental Saga Doriado

Another Secret Rare that should be sought after for combo shenanigans has to be Elemental Saga Doriado. It can be easily searched via Rciela, Sinister Soul of the White Forest and gives the user the ability to reborn any monster as long as you have the required attributes. Then you also get to summon another monster with a different attribute from your Deck! It's important to note that for some reason, they decided to also make Elemental Saga Doriado's effect something neither player can respond to, which makes it not lose out to something like Ghost Belle & Haunted Mansion, Dominus Impulse or D.D. Crow.

We should be glad that Protectcode Talker, Magicians' Souls and Zenna's Deceiving Doll Maidens got banned recently as otherwise this would be another tool to send off Magicians' Souls and then add back later with Firewall Dragon to summon whatever you sent off the Doll Maidens later on. I'm sure there's probably another combo to utilize Elemental Saga Doriado in the Fairy Tail or Magistus Spellcaster combo deck. By using Summon Sorceress and either Endymion, the Crescent of Magistus to equip and return the Doriado to the hand or Charmer Quartet in Bloom to summon it, it's just a matter of how many Attributes you can have in rotation to make Doriado live.

Braving the Beyond

Some might tell you that Beyond the Brave is more like a Genesys set than Advanced, which is partially true considering how the meta is forming with the power level of the newer cards. But compared to how other core sets have done before, I think Beyond the Brave still has its merits especially with how popular the Genesys format is.

On the other hand, the new Angelechy cards are proving themselves to be very meta relevant in both Advanced and Genesys so those cards might just hold up the value of this set alongside The Great Gallant Bandit. I personally am also excited to play with them since they do offer a pretty unique gameplay and resolving Angelechy Opening to e4 on the opponent's first turn is pretty crazy.

Hanko Chow

With crazy combos and ludicrous locks, Hanko Chow's unique deckbuilding style makes him a one-of-a-kind competitor, always looking for a better strategy to beat the best. View Full Bio

item.title: The Biggest Price Spikes in Magic: The Gathering This Week - 10/22/2026

The Biggest Price Spikes in Magic: The Gathering This Week - 10/22/2026

Three things in life are certain; death, taxes, and $60 Jaces.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 22, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

The Theorist, Jace Beleren is how much?

The star of Reality Fracture, both in his fractured reality and our reality as well, The Theorist has done nothing but climb since the set's release two weeks ago. It came out of the gates selling at a cool $50, but in the time since then it actually climbed all the way up to $70 throughout the weekend before dropping off.

But the card is clearly powerful, and likely to be a staple in several decks in both current and future Standard along with the upcoming rotation with the release of Nauctis: The Sunken Realm in early 2027. I think it probably also has legs in Modern — drawing a card every turn is an effect worth spending Solitudes and Force of Negations along with some casual overlap. While the price is currently on the way down as more Reality Fracture is opened, I think we're looking at 2-3 years of Jace being a very playable Standard card at a minimum.

This list packs a lot of power into a Standard deck, and really pushes its synergies to the maximum limit. Obviously Jace is a powerhouse here, but Dimir Uldaros also maintains the engine of Superior Spider-Man and Deceit, powered along by Overlord of the Balemurk. This build also incorporates Uldaros Theorix, which is another Reality Fracture card that's wildly powerful and yet is very affordable right now at $3 per copy.

There's other Standard developments worth highlighting, too.

This Orzhov Lifegain deck is everything I want to do in Standard right now. It is basically enabled by Liliana the Faultless and the ultra-powerful Enlightened Confidant, but this list really pulls pretty evenly from across a handful of sets in Standard including Bloomburrow and The Lost Caverns of Ixalan. And it's got the coolest enchantment to see Standard play in a hot minute. 

The bar for a two-mana enchantment that isn't Up the Beanstalk or a removal spell to see play is absurdly high, and up until this play in its lifetime in Standard the conditions just weren't right for the Bloomburrow rare Lunar Convocation to see the light of day. But now that package is here  — if only in full for a few months before rotation — the deck is good, and the price of the two-mana enchantment is steady climbing.

Lunar Convocation is up this week to an all-time high of $3-4. While that may not sound like much, this enchantment was a bulk rare two weeks ago. It goes to show that Standard, in the midst of RCQ season, still has plenty of legs. Another standout of this deck is Haliya, Guided by Light from Edge of Eternities, which is unsurprisingly on the rise as well, reaching an all-time high of $6 this week.

But enough about Standard, what about Modern?

Modern has been getting a ton of attention recently, with a string of Spotlights events and Regional Championships all bringing high-profile showcases of the very deep format. The story of the season was undoubtedly the rise of Mono-Green Broodscale, but there were plenty of other developments as well that we'll likely see more at the first Pro Tour of 2027 in Detroit, which happens to be another Modern event.

Moonshadow has been a big winner of the last few releases, and Dark Matter Manipulator appears to be something of a gamechanger for the formerly fringe archetype. It's certainly been one of the financial winners from Reality Fracture, climbing from a dollar upon release to $7 today, suddenly making it one of the best rare pulls from a pack.

Moonshadow, meanwhile, has been more of a steady gainer pretty much since the Lorwyn Eclipsed mythic rare reached its post-release low of $9 back in May. It started climbing back up from there, and hit $15 by the beginning of September. Now it's up to $20 as the archetype continues to put up results in Modern — a handful of players all made Day 2 with the deck at the ultra-competitive United States Regional Championships in Los Angeles a few weeks ago.

Is it a reason to dig Detective's Phoenix out of your bulk boxes? Maybe, but the price on the rest of the deck hasn't significantly moved on the latest breakout Modern archetype. However, I'll note that Fear of Missing Out has climbed from its low of $2.50 back up to $4 over the last two months. I don't know if there's much to really note there, but this does look like the most stable home for the card in Modern.

The Best of the Rest

It's not often that I get to bring up cEDH in this column, but the ultra-spikey four-player Commander stack shenanigans that is Bracket 5 Commander has an extremely dedicated player base across the world. As wild as it might sound for a 100-card singleton format built on randomness to develop anything close to a "solved" metagame, that's sort of what has happened at various times over the last few years, thanks to the dedicated work of known players like Sam Black and thousands more unknown players across the globe. It's rare that something comes along that threatens to reorganize the top decks, but there's been plenty of discussion — and from my understanding, some early results — surrounding Dack Fayden, Helping Hand.

There are multiple ways to build the deck that result in a resolved Dack Fayden, Helping Hand winning the game instantly, and while most of them are too complicated for me too easily explain in a column (or understand at all), one of the biggest beneficiaries of Dack's debut — Dack itself is a bulk rare — is Preston, the Vanisher.

One printing only for Preston, the Vanisher, in Jumpstart 2022. If you're thinking that sounds like a recipe for an extremely expensive card under the right conditions, then you're right — and these are the right conditions.

Preston has actually been through a series of spikes over the last couple of years on its way to its current (exploding) price of $55-60 in live listings. When it was printed, Preston ran around $10 and stayed there until late 2024, when it underwent a drastic climb up to $30. It then moved again in March earlier this year, climbing up to $40 for the first time. Now it's well above that, and it's all thanks to Dack. Radiant Solar is another that's creeping up in price due to Dack Fayden, and it's one of the few creatures played in this hyper-competitive deck.

Consider this your weekly Sphinx check-in. If you're not familiar, the entire class of cards has been climbing price thanks to the printing of The Ur-Sphinx, which has catapulted the creature type into the attention sphere for pretty much the first time in the game's history. Magister Sphinx has several printings beyond its original Conflux including Double Masters 2022.

Well, all versions of Magister Sphinx are out of the bulk bin. In fact, you're now looking at $5+ for a copy of the life-setting flyer, so take a look in your extra cards for any Sphinxes you might have laying around — Sphinx Ambassador is $50!

That's all the space I have this week — see you next time as we track more of Reality Fracture's impact in Standard, including at the Magic Spotlight event I'll be covering this weekend in Hartford!

item.title: The Best Steals and Deals From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|budget|finance

The Best Steals and Deals From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

Magic real estate at dollar prices.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Oct 22, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Even with some distance from Reality Fracture's release, we're all trying to be more mindful with our spending these days. Despite the sheer size of Reality Fracture and the continued attention surrounding it, knowing what you should buy can be a puzzle to solve in itself.

Whenever I look through a set such as this one, I always keep an eye out for budget buys that won't break the bank but are likely to see long-term casual and/or competitive play. Prioritizing how much you'll play the card over how much it's actually worth will help you figure out how to use your budget best. Magic Finance isn't always about flipping cards to make a few extra bucks, as it can also be a useful budgeting tool to help you save some cash. Ultimately the goal is to be smart with your spending while still interacting with the latest releases.

The Best Steals and Deals From Reality Fracture

Today, I'll be sifting through some of the best budget buys you can find in Reality Fracture right now. The set has been out for a while which means prices are beginning to settle as more cards continue to enter circulation. The set's incredibly popular, which means there's plenty of supply to meet demand which also means you can find a good deal or two.

Ajani's Anguish

I don't know about you, but I like having access to cards that can encourage a swift end to games in Commander. Ajani's Anguish is one of these, which comes with a Fireball-like effect to deal damage to any target equal to the amount of mana spent to cast it. Upon resolving, the card simply grants every creature you control with trample.

This is a notable get for any Commander strategy that cares about creatures and turning them sideways. Garruk's Uprising is a wildly popular card due to the passive card draw it provides while also granting trample to the board, whereas this one attaches some scalable removal for good measure. I'm generally a fan of cards such as Ajani's Anguish, and it is an elegant way to spit out more keywords if needed. Furthermore, you can just generate a ton of mana and go face with the enchantment. It ain't fancy, but being aggressive rarely is in Commander. 

Multiply by Zero

Multiply by Zero accompanies the elegant class of two mana removal spells geared for competitive play. This one is a little different though, as Multiply by Zero forces a creature to become a 0/0 and leads to the target dying from state-based actions. While it's not the catch-all removal spell we're used to seeing in Magic these days, it is a pretty solid answer to any creature that doesn't have any +1/+1 counters or benefiting from any passive boosts on the battlefield. However, Multiply by Zero does comfortably answer any indestructible creature which is key takeaway here. 

While Standard rotation doesn't trigger until Nauctis: The Sunken Realms' release in February next year, picking up a few copies of Multiply by Zero to prepare for the upcoming rotation may be a smart move to take. Outlaws of Thunder Junctions' Shoot the Sheriff does leave when rotation triggers, meaning players will be seeking out the next best alternative for Standard play.

Tarmogoyf

Oh, how the mighty have fallen. 

While I usually focus on casual and competitive uses when covering cards from a set such as Reality Fracture, I'd be remiss not to mention one of the game's most iconic creatures. Tarmogoyf has had such a colorful history over the years, and now you can own a bit of Magic's history for about a buck. It's crazy to think of the decline over the last decade, since Tarmogoyf was once a $100 card at the height of popularity.

Tarmogoyf doesn't see a ton of play these days, but could have its uses in Standard and Pioneer depending on metagame shifts. That said, if you play Disa the Restless in Commander, you now have an accessible way to stock up on Tarmogoyf tokens if you're short on them.

Lich's Relic

A card I think is currently underrated for Commander is Lich's Relic, which plays into the popular role of Equipment archetypes in the format. Being able to control the battlefield is one of the many ways to succeed in Commander, and the Relic makes it so you can destroy up to one target creature or planeswalker for each opponent you have. Combine this with a Ghostly Flicker or similar, and you have a recipe to manage any threats you may encounter on the battlefield. Sure, you do have to pay two mana each time when the Relic enters, but paying so little mana to answer three creatures/planeswalkers is a seriously good rate. 

Geist of Saint Thalia

If there was a card from Reality Fracture I would crown as the best deal of them all, it would be Geist of Saint Thalia. Thalia reduces the cost of noncreature spells you cast by one generic mana, which means she's ideal for any strategy that has a high density of noncreature spells — and let me tell you, there's a lot of them.

She's especially potent in Artifact archetypes as she's another copy of Etherium Sculptor with further upside, but the possibilities are endless for her in Commander. Thalia also happens to be the best cost reducers printed at two mana at the time of writing, which means this a nice one to have a few copies of in the collection. 

Pompous Battlemage 

Pompous Battlemage has seen plenty of competitive interest which led to some aggressive price swings as of late, but have since relaxed. Even though prices have come down, I feel it's a card you should still pick up if you're looking to play competitively in the coming months. Slickshot Show-Off rotates early next year, which means the Battlemage may become a suitable replacement if you're someone who regularly plays Izzet Prowess or Mono-Red Aggro in Standard.

What I like most about this card is how it itself can trigger prowess while giving you redundancy if you have one too many lands in the mid-to-late-game. You are missing out on some early speed compared to something like Monastery Swiftspear or Slickshot Show-Off, but having access to a cheap one-time spell makes up for it in my opinion. 

The Slow Lands

Reprinted in Reality Fracture are the Slow Lands, which provides another opportunity to snap up Overgrown Farmland, Deserted Beach, Haunted Ridge, Shipwreck Marsh and Rockfall Vale for a cheaper price. These were first printed in Innistrad: Midnight Hunt five years ago, becoming fairly expensive as they enter play untapped if you control two or more other lands. Now with another needed-reprint, it's a good time to stock up on playables if you're wanting versatile mana for Commander or want to prepare for upcoming competitive events. 

Reflecting Pool

Having access to good mana is important in Commander, even though I'll maintain that you probably aren't running enough basic lands. That said, the Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck has some nice reprints, with Reflecting Pool being the best of the bunch. This card has been sneakily creeping up in price over the years which also happens to align with the growing popularity of Commander, as players seek out the best mana options to complement their decks. At the time of writing, it's this particular printing from Reality Fracture that's the cheapest and it isn't remotely close. If there's one thing about Reflecting Pool if reprints in Edge of Eternities were anything to go by, the card's price will rebound as demand will slowly outstrip supply.

The Turbulent Lands

The Turbulent Lands are a recent cycle of cards that first debuted in Secrets of Strixhaven with Reality Fracture adding a few more to support more two-color pairs. Turbulent Crater, Turbulent Shore, and Turbulent Wetlands are the ones available this time around, with prices looking reasonable if you're wanting to add any to your collection. 

A barometer that's worth using here is checking the prices of the Secrets of Strixhaven printings, which happen to be climbing towards the $6-8 mark six months after release. While it's unclear if these ones in Reality Fracture will meet the same trend, they're still pretty affordable in the grand scheme of things. What makes these Turbulent Lands so good for Commander is they can often enter play untapped with the bonus of coming with a subtype, meaning they can be searched up with a Fetch Land or a ramp spell that asks for a specific land type such as Farseek.

item.title: Everything We Know About Pokémon TCG: Delta Reign
item.description:
Pokémon|news

Everything We Know About Pokémon TCG: Delta Reign

Mega Rayquaza will descend from the sky on November 6.

By Peter Day

|

Published Oct 9, 2026

|

3 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

On November 6, 2026, the Mega Evolution Series of the Pokémon TCG will continue its celebration of the Mega Pokémon from Pokémon Legends: Z-A with the release of its newest expansion: Delta Reign.

Like Chaos Rising and Pitch Black earlier in 2026, Delta Reign will be a regular Pokémon expansion mostly adapted from a single Japanese set—in this case, Storm Emeralda. The reasonable set size of 135+ cards will be good news for fans hoping to pull any of the four versions of Mega Rayquaza ex, the crown jewel of the set for collectors and the most exciting new deck centerpiece for players.

Here's everything we know so far about Mega Evolution—Delta Reign.

When Does Delta Reign Release?

Delta Reign will release on November 6, 2026, with Prerelease events held at local game stores starting on October 24. The cards in Delta Reign will be legal to play two weeks after release, starting on November 20.

All Delta Reign products are expected to be available immediately when the set releases. This includes Booster Boxes, Elite Trainer Boxes, Booster Bundles, and various blister packs. Delta Reign Build & Battle Boxes will be available early, at Prerelease events.

Which Pokémon Are in Delta Reign?

Delta Reign will largely feature international versions of the cards from the Japanese set Storm Emeralda.

The headliner Pokémon of Delta Reign will be Mega Rayquaza ex, the strongest new attacker in the set with three different Secret Rare versions to collect. Besides Mega Rayquaza, Delta Reign features powerful or collectible cards for Raikou, Talonflame, Mega Malamar, Groudon, Kyogre, Growlithe, and Azurill.

While the full set list has yet to be revealed, The Pokémon Company International has confirmed the set will include:

  • Four Mega Evolution Pokémon ex.
  • Six Pokémon ex.
  • Six Stadium cards creating three Legendary Stadiums.
  • 14 Illustration Rare Pokémon.
  • 17 Ultra Rare Pokémon and Trainer cards.
  • Six Special Illustration Rare Pokémon and Supporter cards.

If the full set matches the expected breakdown, the following Pokémon will all have full-art cards in Chaos Rising:

  • Mega Rayquaza
  • Mega Golurk
  • Mega Malamar
  • Mega Golisopod
  • Raikou
  • Groudon
  • Kyogre
  • Kecleon
  • Growlithe
  • Azurill
  • Altaria
  • Inkay
  • Electivire
  • Magmortar
  • Pincurchin
  • Enamorus
  • Masquerain
  • Talonflame
  • Wishiwashi
  • Heat Rotom

What Is a Legendary Stadium?

Delta Reign will introduce a new mechanic to the Pokémon TCG: Legendary Stadiums.

A Legendary Stadium is a powerful Stadium split across two cards. Similar to old Pokémon LEGEND cards like Suicune & Entei LEGEND (Top) and (Bottom), you have to have both halves of a Legendary Stadium in your hand in order to play them as a single game object. If the game rules or a card effect would discard a Legendary Stadium, both halves of the Stadium go to the discard pile.

There are three Legendary Stadiums in Delta Reign, each made of two cards: Legendary Pyroduct, Legendary Trench, and Legendary Summit.

What Are the Chase Cards in Delta Reign?

Mega Rayquaza is unquestionably the star of Delta Reign. The most valuable card in the set will be the Special Illustration Rare version of Mega Rayquaza ex, followed by the Mega Hyper Rare "gold" version of the same card. 

The Japanese version of these cards are currently the most valuable cards in Storm Emeralda by a wide margin.

Rayquaza has a long history of appearing on expensive Pokémon cards, going back to Rayquaza ex from EX Dragon in 2003. While the Sky-High Pokémon had to share the spotlight with Umbreon and other Eeveelutions in Evolving Skies, Delta Reign belongs entirely to Mega Rayquaza ex—no other Pokémon in the set can compete with Rayquaza for name recognition and high-rarity treatments.

What Are the Best Cards in Delta Reign?

Mega Rayquaza ex looks to be the best new attacker coming out of Delta Reign. With built-in Energy acceleration and an attack that scales to KO any opponent, Mega Rayquaza ex has the makings of a serious contender.

It has weaknesses (including a literal Lightning weakness) that have caused it to fall off in the Japanese metagame compared to when it first released. But in the right format, it could still shine.

Talonflame ex's Excited Dive Ability lets players drop it directly into play as long as they have a Colorless Mega Evolution Pokémon ex. Mega Rayquaza ex fits the bill, but most Japanese players have paired Talonflame ex with Mega Kangaskhan ex for a dynamic duo that both hit hard while drawing or searching cards. Its free Retreat Cost helps Talonflame ex keep up in the Basic Box decks that run Latias ex.
